items.stem: Marginal revenue product of labour is
options: the extra output from one more worker
the extra revenue a firm earns from employing one more worker
the wage paid to the last worker
total revenue divided by the number of workers
items.answer: the extra revenue a firm earns from employing one more worker
items.markingKey: MRP = MPP × MR (= MPP × P in a competitive product market).

items.stem: Explain why the MRP curve slopes downwards.
items.answer: Because of diminishing marginal returns, each extra worker adds less output (falling MPP); with imperfect competition, MR also falls as output rises; so MRP = MPP × MR falls.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: diminishing MPP; 1 mark: MRP = MPP × MR [2]

items.stem: Explain two factors that affect the wage elasticity of demand for labour.
items.answer: Ease of substituting capital; PED for the final product; proportion of labour in total costs; time period.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each identified, 1 mark each explained [4]

items.stem: A firm sells shirts at $5 each in a competitive market. Workers: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; Total product (shirts per day): 26, 46, 62, 75, 85, 89. Calculate the marginal revenue product of worker 3.

A firm sells shirts at $12 each in a competitive product market and hires labour in a competitive labour market at $126 per worker per day. Workers: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; Total product (shirts per day): 27, 51, 74, 86, 97, 104. Calculate the MRP of each worker and the profit-maximising number of workers. The product price then rises to $16. Explain the effect on the demand for labour and calculate the new employment.
items.answer: MRP: 324, 288, 276, 144, 132, 84. Employ 5 workers: the last worker hired has MRP ≥ $126; the next has MRP below the wage. At $16, MRP rises (shifts right), so employment rises to 5.
items.markingKey: MPP = ΔTP [1]; MRP = MPP × P [1]; hire while MRP ≥ W [1]; 5 workers [1]. New MRP = MPP × 16; employment 5 [2].

items.stem: A firm sells printed books at $12 each in a competitive product market and hires labour in a competitive labour market at $126 per worker per day. Workers: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; Total product (printed books per day): 24, 46, 60, 71, 76, 79. Calculate the MRP of each worker and the profit-maximising number of workers. The product price then rises to $17. Explain the effect on the demand for labour and calculate the new employment.
items.answer: MRP: 288, 264, 168, 132, 60, 36. Employ 4 workers: the last worker hired has MRP ≥ $126; the next has MRP below the wage. At $17, MRP rises (shifts right), so employment rises to 4.
items.markingKey: MPP = ΔTP [1]; MRP = MPP × P [1]; hire while MRP ≥ W [1]; 4 workers [1]. New MRP = MPP × 17; employment 4 [2].

items.stem: Extract: Gorvania will raise its national minimum wage from $8 to $10 an hour. Employers in retail and hospitality warn that up to 30,000 jobs may be lost; unions argue that many employers have monopsony power. (a) Calculate the percentage increase in the minimum wage. (b) With the aid of a diagram, explain why employers predict job losses.
items.answer: (a) 25% (b) Competitive market: wage above equilibrium, employment falls to Ld, unemployment Ls − Ld.

items.stem: Extract: Dravonia will raise its national minimum wage from $7 to $9 an hour. Employers in retail and hospitality warn that up to 50,000 jobs may be lost; unions argue that many employers have monopsony power. (a) Calculate the percentage increase in the minimum wage. (b) Discuss whether a higher minimum wage is the best way to reduce in-work poverty.
items.answer: (a) 28.6% (b) Raises pay for low-paid; may cut hours/jobs, raise prices; poorly targeted on households; alternatives: tax credits, training.

items.stem: Explain two limitations of marginal revenue product theory.
items.answer: Hard to measure the MPP of individual workers, especially in teams or services; many workers are in the public sector without a market price; wages are influenced by unions, custom and discrimination.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each identified, 1 mark each explained [4]

items.stem: The wage elasticity of supply of labour measures
options: the change in wages when prices rise
the number of hours worked per week
the responsiveness of labour demand to the wage
the responsiveness of the quantity of labour supplied to a change in the wage rate
items.answer: the responsiveness of the quantity of labour supplied to a change in the wage rate
items.markingKey: %ΔQs labour ÷ %Δwage.

items.stem: Explain the income and substitution effects of a wage rise on the hours an individual wants to work.
items.answer: Substitution effect: leisure becomes more expensive (higher opportunity cost), so the worker supplies more hours. Income effect: with higher income the worker can afford more leisure, so supplies fewer hours. The net effect depends on which is larger.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each effect; 1 mark net effect [3]

items.stem: Explain two non-wage factors that influence the supply of labour to an occupation.
items.answer: Working conditions; job security; training and qualifications; status; fringe benefits; location; flexibility.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each identified, 1 mark each explained [4]

items.stem: When the hourly wage of bus drivers in Umbria Nova rose from $12 to $15, the number willing to work rose from 2,000 to 2200. Calculate the wage elasticity of supply of labour.

When the hourly wage of hotel staff in Selmaria rose from $10 to $12, the number willing to work rose from 4,000 to 4600. Calculate the wage elasticity of supply of labour and explain two reasons why the supply of labour to this occupation might be inelastic.
items.answer: WES = 15%/20% = 0.75 (inelastic). Long training/qualifications, vocation-specific skills, geographical immobility, short time period.
items.markingKey: % changes [1]; WES = 0.75 [1]; two reasons consistent with the value [2].

items.stem: Extract: Westaria will raise its national minimum wage from $8 to $10 an hour. Employers in retail and hospitality warn that up to 20,000 jobs may be lost; unions argue that many employers have monopsony power. (a) Calculate the percentage increase in the minimum wage. (b) Explain why unions argue that employment may not fall.
items.answer: (a) 25% (b) In monopsony, a minimum wage between Wm and the competitive wage raises both wage and employment.

items.stem: A monopsonist in a labour market
options: is a single seller of labour
is the single buyer of labour and pays a lower wage and employs fewer workers than a competitive market
pays a wage equal to MRP
employs more workers than a competitive market
items.answer: is the single buyer of labour and pays a lower wage and employs fewer workers than a competitive market
items.markingKey: MCL > ALS; employs where MCL = MRP, pays wage from supply curve.

items.stem: With the aid of a diagram, explain how wages and employment are determined in a monopsony labour market.
items.answer: Diagram: wage on vertical axis, labour horizontal. Upward-sloping supply (ACL); MCL above and steeper; downward-sloping MRP. Employment Lm where MCL = MRP; wage Wm read from supply curve at Lm, below MRP. Compared with competitive equilibrium (MRP = supply), wage and employment are lower.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: curves; 1 mark: MCL = MRP; 1 mark: wage from supply; 1 mark: comparison [4]

items.stem: Explain how a trade union could raise wages in a competitive labour market and the likely effect on employment.
items.answer: By collective bargaining or restricting labour supply; the wage rises above equilibrium, so employers move up their MRP curve and employ fewer workers; the fall in employment is larger if labour demand is wage elastic.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: method; 1 mark: wage above equilibrium; 1 mark: employment falls depending on elasticity [3]

items.stem: A monopsony employer faces this labour supply schedule: Workers: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7; Wage needed to attract this many ($ per day): 60, 70, 80, 90, 100, 110, 120; MRP ($): 135, 120, 105, 90, 75, 60, 45. Calculate the marginal cost of employing worker 3.

A monopsony employer faces this labour market: Workers: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7; Wage needed to attract this many ($ per day): 60, 80, 100, 120, 140, 160, 180; MRP ($): 240, 220, 200, 180, 160, 140, 120. (a) Calculate the total and marginal cost of labour. (b) Identify the profit-maximising employment and wage. (c) Compare with the outcome if the market were competitive.
items.answer: (a) TCL: 60, 160, 300, 480, 700, 960, 1260; MCL: 60, 100, 140, 180, 220, 260, 300 (b) 4 workers (MCL ≤ MRP), wage $120 (from supply) (c) Competitive: employ where wage = MRP: 5 workers at about $140; monopsony employs fewer and pays less.
items.markingKey: (a) TCL = W × L, MCL = ΔTCL [2]; (b) MCL = MRP, wage read from supply [2]; (c) competitive outcome where supply = MRP; comparison [2].

items.stem: A monopsony employer faces this labour market: Workers: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7; Wage needed to attract this many ($ per day): 50, 70, 90, 110, 130, 150, 170; MRP ($): 220, 205, 190, 175, 160, 145, 130. (a) Calculate the total and marginal cost of labour. (b) Identify the profit-maximising employment and wage. (c) Compare with the outcome if the market were competitive.
items.answer: (a) TCL: 50, 140, 270, 440, 650, 900, 1190; MCL: 50, 90, 130, 170, 210, 250, 290 (b) 4 workers (MCL ≤ MRP), wage $110 (from supply) (c) Competitive: employ where wage = MRP: 5 workers at about $130; monopsony employs fewer and pays less.
items.markingKey: (a) TCL = W × L, MCL = ΔTCL [2]; (b) MCL = MRP, wage read from supply [2]; (c) competitive outcome where supply = MRP; comparison [2].

items.stem: Extract: Marvona will raise its national minimum wage from $7 to $9 an hour. Employers in retail and hospitality warn that up to 20,000 jobs may be lost; unions argue that many employers have monopsony power. (a) Calculate the percentage increase in the minimum wage. (b) Explain why unions argue that employment may not fall.
items.answer: (a) 28.6% (b) In monopsony, a minimum wage between Wm and the competitive wage raises both wage and employment.

items.stem: Extract: Halvoria will raise its national minimum wage from $7 to $8.5 an hour. Employers in retail and hospitality warn that up to 30,000 jobs may be lost; unions argue that many employers have monopsony power. (a) With the aid of a diagram, explain why employers predict job losses. (b) Explain two factors that determine how many jobs are lost.
items.answer: (a) Competitive market: wage above equilibrium, employment falls to Ld, unemployment Ls − Ld. (b) Wage elasticity of demand for labour (substitutes, labour share of costs, PED of product), size of rise relative to equilibrium, state of economy.

items.stem: Transfer earnings are
options: the minimum payment needed to keep a factor of production in its current use
payments made by the government
the total wage bill
earnings above the minimum needed to keep a factor in its use
items.answer: the minimum payment needed to keep a factor of production in its current use
items.markingKey: Equal to what it could earn in its next best alternative.

items.stem: Explain why top football players earn a large amount of economic rent.
items.answer: Their talent is scarce and supply is very inelastic; demand (MRP) from clubs is high, so their wages far exceed what they could earn in their next best job (transfer earnings).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: inelastic supply/scarce talent; 1 mark: high demand; 1 mark: wage far above transfer earnings [3]

items.stem: With the aid of a diagram, explain the difference between transfer earnings and economic rent.
items.answer: Diagram: upward-sloping supply of labour and demand curve; equilibrium wage W and employment L. The area under the supply curve up to L is transfer earnings; the area above the supply curve and below W is economic rent.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: diagram; 1 mark: transfer earnings area; 1 mark: economic rent area [3]

items.stem: Isla, a famous singer, earns $200 thousand a year. Their best alternative job would pay $80 thousand. Calculate the economic rent Isla earns.
items.answer: $120 thousand
items.markingKey: Economic rent = earnings − transfer earnings = 200 − 80 = 120 thousand.

items.stem: The supply curve of accountants is W = 15 + 0.005L, where W is the hourly wage in $ and L the number of workers. The equilibrium wage is $27.5 with 2,500 workers employed. Calculate total hourly earnings, transfer earnings and economic rent.
items.answer: Total = $68,750; transfer earnings = $53,125; economic rent = $15,625.

items.stem: Extract: Merania will raise its national minimum wage from $7 to $8.5 an hour. Employers in retail and hospitality warn that up to 20,000 jobs may be lost; unions argue that many employers have monopsony power. (a) Calculate the percentage increase in the minimum wage. (b) With the aid of a diagram, explain why employers predict job losses.
items.answer: (a) 21.4% (b) Competitive market: wage above equilibrium, employment falls to Ld, unemployment Ls − Ld.

items.stem: A national minimum wage set above the equilibrium wage in a competitive labour market is likely to
options: raise employment
reduce the supply of labour
reduce employment and create unemployment
have no effect
items.answer: reduce employment and create unemployment
items.markingKey: Ls > Ld at the minimum wage.

items.stem: With the aid of a diagram, explain how a minimum wage can increase employment in a monopsony.
items.answer: Diagram: ACL (supply), MCL above it and MRP. Without intervention: L1 where MCL = MRP, wage W1 from supply. A minimum wage Wmin above W1 makes the firm’s MCL horizontal at Wmin up to the supply curve; employment rises to where Wmin meets supply (or MRP), with a higher wage.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: monopsony equilibrium; 1 mark: Wmin creates horizontal MCL; 1 mark: higher employment and wage [3]

items.stem: Explain two reasons for the gender pay gap.
items.answer: Occupational segregation (women concentrated in lower-paid sectors); career breaks and part-time work; discrimination; fewer women in senior roles.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each identified, 1 mark each explained [4]

items.stem: In a competitive labour market for unskilled workers, demand is Ld = 16,800 − 400W and supply is Ls = 8,400 + 300W (W in $ per hour). The government sets a minimum wage of $13. Calculate the unemployment created by the minimum wage.
items.answer: 700 workers

items.stem: In a competitive labour market for unskilled workers, demand is Ld = 13,800 − 300W and supply is Ls = 10,800 + 200W (W in $ per hour). The government sets a minimum wage of $8. Calculate the equilibrium wage and employment, employment at the minimum wage, the number of jobs lost and the unemployment created. Explain why these two figures differ.
items.answer: Equilibrium W = $6, L = 12,000; at $8: employed 11,400, jobs lost 600, unemployment 1,000. Unemployment exceeds jobs lost because the higher wage also attracts 400 extra people into the labour market.
items.markingKey: Equilibrium [1]; Ld at Wmin [1]; jobs lost = 12,000 − 11,400 [1]; unemployment = Ls − Ld [1]; extra supply explanation [1].

items.stem: Extract: Nordavia will raise its national minimum wage from $6 to $8 an hour. Employers in retail and hospitality warn that up to 30,000 jobs may be lost; unions argue that many employers have monopsony power. (a) Calculate the percentage increase in the minimum wage. (b) Explain why unions argue that employment may not fall.
items.answer: (a) 33.3% (b) In monopsony, a minimum wage between Wm and the competitive wage raises both wage and employment.

items.stem: A profit-maximising firm in a competitive labour market employs workers up to the point where
options: the wage equals average revenue product
the wage equals the marginal revenue product
marginal product is at its maximum
total product is maximised
items.answer: the wage equals the marginal revenue product
items.markingKey: Hire while MRP ≥ W; MRP curve is the firm’s demand for labour.

items.stem: Demand for bicycles in Loristan falls sharply. Explain why workers who make bicycles may lose their jobs or see lower wages.
items.answer: Labour demand is derived: lower product demand reduces price/MR, so MRP falls and the labour demand curve shifts left, reducing wages and/or employment.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: derived demand; 1 mark: MRP falls → labour demand shifts left [2]

items.stem: A firm sells boxes of fruit at $8 each in a competitive market. Workers: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; Total product (boxes of fruit per day): 22, 43, 61, 74, 85, 95. Calculate the marginal revenue product of worker 3.

A firm sells printed books at $5 each in a competitive product market and hires labour in a competitive labour market at $138 per worker per day. Workers: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; Total product (printed books per day): 29, 57, 83, 106, 124, 128. Calculate the MRP of each worker and the profit-maximising number of workers.
items.answer: MRP: 145, 140, 130, 115, 90, 20. Employ 2 workers: the last worker hired has MRP ≥ $138; the next has MRP below the wage.
items.markingKey: MPP = ΔTP [1]; MRP = MPP × P [1]; hire while MRP ≥ W [1]; 2 workers [1].

items.stem: (a) Explain how the demand for labour is derived from marginal revenue product. (b) Consider whether marginal revenue product theory fully explains the wages paid to workers.
items.answer: (a) Explanation of the theory (with a described diagram where relevant), drawing on: Wages reflect productivity and product price; derived demand. (b) Case for the view: Wages reflect productivity and product price; derived demand. Case against / evaluation: Hard to measure MRP; public sector; unions, monopsony, discrimination, minimum wages, custom and practice also set wages. Conclusion: a judgement on the conditions under which the view holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Knowledge and understanding of the theory, clear analytical chain; diagram described accurately with labelled axes and curves. (b) Analysis of arguments for and against; evaluation reaches a justified conclusion that weighs the conditions under which the claim holds. Top level needs a judgement, not just a summary.

items.stem: A backward-bending individual labour supply curve occurs when
options: wages fall
the firm is a monopsonist
the substitution effect outweighs the income effect
the income effect of a higher wage outweighs the substitution effect
items.answer: the income effect of a higher wage outweighs the substitution effect
items.markingKey: At high wages workers buy more leisure.

items.stem: Explain why a large rise in wages for pharmaceutical workers in Umbria Nova might lead some existing workers to work fewer hours.
items.answer: The income effect: higher wages mean the same income can be earned in fewer hours, so workers may buy more leisure; if this outweighs the substitution effect, the individual supply curve bends backwards.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: income effect; 1 mark: outweighs substitution effect [2]

items.stem: When the hourly wage of bus drivers in Valdoria rose from $25 to $27.5, the number willing to work rose from 5,000 to 5500. Calculate the wage elasticity of supply of labour.

Extract: Tarvia will raise its national minimum wage from $6 to $8 an hour. Employers in retail and hospitality warn that up to 20,000 jobs may be lost; unions argue that many employers have monopsony power. (a) With the aid of a diagram, explain why employers predict job losses. (b) Explain why unions argue that employment may not fall.
items.answer: (a) Competitive market: wage above equilibrium, employment falls to Ld, unemployment Ls − Ld. (b) In monopsony, a minimum wage between Wm and the competitive wage raises both wage and employment.

items.stem: For a monopsonist, the marginal cost of labour is above the wage because
options: workers are paid different wages
labour supply is perfectly elastic
it is a price taker in the labour market
to hire an extra worker it must raise the wage for all its workers
items.answer: to hire an extra worker it must raise the wage for all its workers
items.markingKey: Upward-sloping supply of labour to the firm.

items.stem: Fenwick & Co is the only large employer in a small town in Zentara. Explain why it may be able to pay lower wages than firms in Bangkok.
items.answer: As a monopsonist it faces an upward-sloping labour supply curve and few alternative employers, so it employs where MCL = MRP and pays the lower wage on the supply curve.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: monopsony/few alternatives; 1 mark: MCL = MRP, wage below MRP [2]

items.stem: In the market for electricians in Lunaria, labour demand is Ld = 4,480 − 40W and labour supply is Ls = 3,760 + 20W, where W is the hourly wage in $. Calculate the equilibrium wage and employment, and explain the effect of an increase in demand for the product these workers make.
items.answer: W = $12, employment = 4,000. Higher product demand raises MRP, shifting labour demand right, so wage and employment both rise.

items.stem: A large mining company is the only major employer in a remote region of Halvoria. (a) With the aid of a diagram, explain how wages and employment are determined in a monopsony labour market. (b) Consider whether trade unions always reduce employment.
items.answer: (a) Explanation of the theory (with a described diagram where relevant), drawing on: In competitive markets, union wages above equilibrium cut employment. (b) Case for the view: In competitive markets, union wages above equilibrium cut employment. Case against / evaluation: Monopsony case: union can raise W and L; productivity gains; reduced turnover; depends on elasticity of labour demand. Conclusion: a judgement on the conditions under which the view holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Knowledge and understanding of the theory, clear analytical chain; diagram described accurately with labelled axes and curves. (b) Analysis of arguments for and against; evaluation reaches a justified conclusion that weighs the conditions under which the claim holds. Top level needs a judgement, not just a summary.

items.stem: Grace earns $90,000 a year as a surgeon in Dhaka but could earn $40,000 as a university lecturer. Explain how much of the salary is transfer earnings and how much is economic rent.
items.answer: Transfer earnings are $40,000 (the next best alternative); economic rent is $90,000 − $40,000 = $50,000.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Explain why a tax on economic rent may not reduce the supply of a factor of production.
items.answer: Economic rent is the surplus above transfer earnings; taking part of it still leaves the factor earning at least its transfer earnings, so it stays in its current use.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: rent above minimum; 1 mark: supply unaffected [2]

items.stem: Mei, a famous singer, earns $400 thousand a year. Their best alternative job would pay $30 thousand. Calculate the economic rent Mei earns.
items.answer: $370 thousand
items.markingKey: Economic rent = earnings − transfer earnings = 400 − 30 = 370 thousand.

items.stem: The government of Gorvania raises the minimum wage by 10%. Explain why the effect on employment in the soft drinks industry depends on the wage elasticity of demand for labour.
items.answer: If demand is wage elastic (labour a large share of costs, easy substitution by machines, elastic product demand), employment falls a lot; if inelastic, few jobs are lost.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: elastic → big fall; 1 mark: determinants [2]

items.stem: In a competitive labour market for unskilled workers, demand is Ld = 23,200 − 400W and supply is Ls = 16,000 + 500W (W in $ per hour). The government sets a minimum wage of $9. Calculate the unemployment created by the minimum wage.
items.answer: 900 workers

items.stem: In a competitive labour market for unskilled workers, demand is Ld = 13,000 − 300W and supply is Ls = 8,000 + 200W (W in $ per hour). The government sets a minimum wage of $13. Calculate the equilibrium wage and employment, employment at the minimum wage, the number of jobs lost and the unemployment created. Explain why these two figures differ.
items.answer: Equilibrium W = $10, L = 10,000; at $13: employed 9,100, jobs lost 900, unemployment 1,500. Unemployment exceeds jobs lost because the higher wage also attracts 600 extra people into the labour market.
items.markingKey: Equilibrium [1]; Ld at Wmin [1]; jobs lost = 10,000 − 9,100 [1]; unemployment = Ls − Ld [1]; extra supply explanation [1].

items.stem: The demand for labour is a derived demand because
options: it is set by the government
labour is demanded for the output it produces
workers demand jobs
it does not depend on wages
items.answer: labour is demanded for the output it produces
items.markingKey: Demand depends on demand for the final product.

items.stem: The supply of labour to a particular occupation is likely to be inelastic when
options: the time period is long
many workers can easily switch into it
long training and specific qualifications are required
the job requires few skills
items.answer: long training and specific qualifications are required
items.markingKey: E.g. surgeons, airline pilots.

items.stem: Explain why the supply of labour to the cinema industry in Muscat is likely to be more elastic in the long run than in the short run.
items.answer: In the long run workers can train, gain qualifications and relocate, and new entrants join the labour force, so supply responds more to a wage change.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: time to train/relocate; 1 mark: more responsive [2]

items.stem: When the hourly wage of bus drivers in Nordavia rose from $15 to $16.5, the number willing to work rose from 4,000 to 4080. Calculate the wage elasticity of supply of labour.
Hospitals in Ostrelia cannot recruit enough nurses despite pay rises. Discuss the extent to which higher wages will always increase the supply of labour.
items.answer: Arguments for: Substitution effect: higher opportunity cost of leisure; more people enter the occupation. Arguments against / evaluation: Income effect and backward-bending supply; non-wage factors; training time; immobility. Conclusion: a supported judgement that depends on the conditions identified.
items.markingKey: Knowledge and analysis (about 60%): accurate theory, logical chains of reasoning and a relevant diagram described with axes, curves and shifts. Evaluation (about 40%): considers both sides, the assumptions and the context, and reaches a justified conclusion.

items.stem: Bilateral monopoly in a labour market means
options: two unions competing
a monopsony employer bargaining with a monopoly trade union
two firms selling labour
a minimum wage set by the government
items.answer: a monopsony employer bargaining with a monopoly trade union
items.markingKey: Wage settled by bargaining between limits.

(b) Discuss whether a higher minimum wage is the best way to reduce in-work poverty.
items.answer: (a) 25% (b) Raises pay for low-paid; may cut hours/jobs, raise prices; poorly targeted on households; alternatives: tax credits, training.

items.stem: Ethan earns $90,000 a year as a surgeon in Lisbon but could earn $40,000 as a university lecturer. Explain how much of the salary is transfer earnings and how much is economic rent.
items.answer: Transfer earnings are $40,000 (the next best alternative); economic rent is $90,000 − $40,000 = $50,000.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Tomás, a famous singer, earns $200 thousand a year. Their best alternative job would pay $50 thousand. Calculate the economic rent Tomás earns.
items.answer: $150 thousand
items.markingKey: Economic rent = earnings − transfer earnings = 200 − 50 = 150 thousand.

items.stem: Workers in dangerous jobs on oil rigs off Istrana earn far more than office workers with similar qualifications. Explain why.
items.answer: A compensating differential: higher pay is needed to attract workers to unpleasant, dangerous, remote work; supply to these jobs is lower at any given wage.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: compensating differential; 1 mark: lower supply/non-wage factors [2]

items.stem: In a competitive labour market for unskilled workers, demand is Ld = 14,000 − 400W and supply is Ls = 7,000 + 300W (W in $ per hour). The government sets a minimum wage of $12. Calculate the unemployment created by the minimum wage.
items.answer: 1,400 workers

items.stem: In a competitive labour market for unskilled workers, demand is Ld = 16,800 − 400W and supply is Ls = 8,400 + 300W (W in $ per hour). The government sets a minimum wage of $15. Calculate the equilibrium wage and employment, employment at the minimum wage, the number of jobs lost and the unemployment created. Explain why these two figures differ.
items.answer: Equilibrium W = $12, L = 12,000; at $15: employed 10,800, jobs lost 1,200, unemployment 2,100. Unemployment exceeds jobs lost because the higher wage also attracts 900 extra people into the labour market.
items.markingKey: Equilibrium [1]; Ld at Wmin [1]; jobs lost = 12,000 − 10,800 [1]; unemployment = Ls − Ld [1]; extra supply explanation [1].
